contract.rules: If the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate (U-3) reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the Employment Situation Report is above 4.4% in September 2026, then the market resolves to Yes.
contract.title: Will the unemployment rate (U-3) be above 4.4% in September?

limitations: Prices are separated from this project, not protected by an operating-system sandbox.
Selection checks spread and top-of-book size only; neither establishes market accuracy.
The agent must verify the event is still unknown; an open market alone cannot establish this.

specification.no: The stated qualifying event does not occur, subject to the frozen contract rules.
specification.text: Will the unemployment rate (U-3) be above 4.4% in September? — Above 4.4%
specification.void: Nonbinary fair-value settlement or a cancelled/invalid contract is excluded from eventual outcome scoring.
specification.yes: If the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate (U-3) reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the Employment Situation Report is above 4.4% in September 2026, then the market resolves to Yes.

specification.contract_match_rationale: Question carries full price-free contract conditions. Deadline conservatively uses market close; evaluate only well before this time and verify unknown outcome separately.
specification.eligibility_rationale: Dated future event or current-day future maximum; active unresolved book required. Outside research must independently check whether the outcome is already known.
specification.method: Question-only versus outside research; independent contexts

assumptions: Independent outside-research arm; not a sequential update of the question-only arm.
payload.rationale: The unemployment rate was 4.1% in August and July, and 4.2% in June. For the September rate to be strictly above 4.4%, it must round to at least 4.5%, requiring a 0.4 percentage point increase in a single month. Given the solid August nonfarm payroll growth of 162,000, the labor market appears relatively stable. A 0.4 percentage point jump in one month is extremely rare and typically only occurs during sudden, severe economic shocks. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is that such a large one-month jump is historically nearly unprecedented without a major crisis, making even a 3% chance generous. The strongest reason it could be too low is the possibility of a sudden, unforeseen economic shock, a severe weather event impacting the September survey week, or a significant statistical anomaly in the household survey data.
uncertainties: Recorded source limitations and unresolved future event.

payload.exposure_notes: No detected target-odds exposure. Forecast workers received only question definitions and their assigned data; no tools. Source screening and separation are procedural, not proof about model pretraining.
payload.stopping_reason: All registered forecast attempts sealed before any target reveal.

pkt_bc68e468ecc37c3620fcaad2:bls_august.claim: The September 4 BLS release reports unemployment of 4.1% in August and July, versus 4.2% in June. August nonfarm payroll growth was 162,000. September's release is scheduled for October 2 at 8:30 a.m. ET.

L183: # Employment Situation News Release
L184: 
L185:     Transmission of material in this news release is embargoed until                       USDL-26-1435
L186:     8:30 a.m. (ET) Friday, September 4, 2026
L187: 
L188:     Technical information:
L189:      Household data:      (202) 691-6378  *  cpsinfo@bls.gov  *  www.bls.gov/cps
L190:      Establishment data:  (202) 691-6555  *  cesinfo@bls.gov  *  www.bls.gov/ces
L191: 
L192:     Media contact:        (202) 691-5902  *  PressOffice@bls.gov
L193:                                 THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - AUGUST 2026
L194: 
L195: 
L196:     Total nonfarm payroll employment increased by 162,000 in August, and the unemployment rate was
L197:     unchanged at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment
L198:     increased in food services and drinking places and in local government education. The
L199:     information industry lost jobs.
L200: 
L201:     This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys. The household survey measures
L202:     labor force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics. The establishment
L203:     survey measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry. For more information
L204:     about the concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical
L205:     Note.
L206: 
L207:     Household Survey Data
L208: 
L209:     The unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.1 percent in August, and the number of unemployed
L210:     people changed little at 7.0 million. Both measures changed little over the year.
L211:     (See table A-1.)
L212: 
L213:     Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rate for people who are Asian declined to 3.2
L214:     percent in August. The rate for teenagers edged up to 14.1 percent over the month, mostly
L215:     offsetting a decline in the prior month. The jobless rates for adult men (4.0 percent), adult
L216:     women (3.5 percent), and people who are White (3.7 percent), Black (6.0 percent), or Hispanic
L217:     (4.8 percent) showed little change in August. (See tables A-1, A-2, and A-3.)
L218: 
L219:     The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more) changed little at 1.9
L220:     million in August. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.0 percent of all unemployed
L221:     people. (See table A-12.)
L222: 
L223:     The labor force participation rate edged up to 61.6 percent in August but is down by 0.5
L224:     percentage point since January. The employment-population ratio, at 59.1 percent, changed
L225:     little over the month and since January. (See table A-1.)
L226: 
L227:     The number of people employed part time for economic reasons decreased by 414,000 to 4.4
L228:     million in August. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were
L229:     working part time because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time
L230:     jobs. (See table A-8.)
L231: 
L232:     In August, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little
L233:     at 5.7 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not
L234:     actively looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take
L235:     a job. (See table A-1.)
L236: 
L237:     Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached
L238:     to the labor force changed little at 1.7 million in August. These individuals wanted and were
L239:     available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked
L240:     for work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of
L241:     the marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, changed little in
L242:     August at 441,000. (See Summary table A.)
L243: 
L244:     Establishment Survey Data
L245: 
L246:     Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 162,000 in August, higher than the average monthly
L247:     gain of 31,000 over the prior 12 months. In August, employment increased in food services and
L248:     drinking places and in local government education. The information industry lost jobs.
L249:     (See table B-1.)
L250: 
L251:     Employment in food services and drinking places increased by 59,000 in August, well above the
L252:     average monthly gain of 12,000 over the prior 12 months.
L253: 
L254:     Local government education added 42,000 jobs in August, largely offsetting a decrease in the
L255:     prior month. Local government education has shown little net change since January 2025.
L256: 
L257:     In August, employment in manufacturing continued its upward trend (+16,000) and is up by
L258:     58,000 since a recent low in December 2025. Employment in machinery manufacturing (+6,000) and
L259:     in fabricated metal product manufacturing (+6,000) continued trending up in August.
L260: 
L261:     Employment in health care continued to trend up in August (+13,000) but at a slower pace than
L262:     the average monthly gain over the prior 12 months (+32,000). Over the month, home health care
L263:     services (+11,000) and hospitals (+8,000) added jobs.
L264: 
L265:     Information employment declined by 23,000 in August, following losses that had averaged 8,000
L266:     per month over the prior 12 months. In August, job losses occurred in computing infrastructure
L267:     providers, data processing, web hosting, and related services (-8,000), in publishing
L268:     industries (-7,000), and in broadcasting and content providers (-5,000).
L269: 
L270:     Construction employment changed little in August (+22,000). Employment in nonresidential
L271:     specialty trade contractors continued to trend up (+8,000), similar to the average monthly
L272:     gain over the prior 12 months (+6,000).
L273: 
L274:     Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining,
L275:     quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; wholesale trade; retail trade; transportation and
L276:     warehousing; financial activities; professional and business services; social assistance; and
L277:     other services.
L278: 
L279:     In August, average hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls rose by 10
L280:     cents, or 0.3 percent, to $37.75. Over the year, average hourly earnings have increased by 3.1
L281:     percent. In August, average hourly earnings of private-sector production and nonsupervisory
L282:     employees rose by 11 cents, or 0.3 percent, to $32.53. (See tables B-3 and B-8.)
L283:     The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls edged up by 0.1 hour to
L284:     34.4 hours in August. In manufacturing, the average workweek edged up by 0.1 hour to 40.5
L285:     hours, and overtime was unchanged at 3.1 hours. The average workweek for production and
L286:     nonsupervisory employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 33.8 hours.
L287:     (See tables B-2 and B-7.)
L288: 
L289:     The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for June was revised up by 11,000, from
L290:     +20,000 to +31,000, and the change for July was revised up by 44,000, from -23,000 to +21,000.
L291:     With these revisions, employment in June and July combined is 55,000 higher than previously
L292:     reported. (Monthly revisions result from additional reports received from businesses and
L293:     government agencies since the last published estimates and from the recalculation of seasonal
L294:     factors.)
L295: 
L296:     _____________
L297:     The Employment Situation for September 2026 is scheduled to be published on Friday,
L298:     October 2, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. (ET).

L419:     Frequently Asked Questions about Employment and Unemployment Estimates
L420: 
L421:     1. Why are there two monthly measures of employment?
L422: 
L423:        The household survey and establishment survey both produce sample-based estimates
L424:        of employment, and both have strengths and limitations. The establishment survey
L425:        employment series has a smaller margin of error on the measurement of month-to-
L426:        month change than the household survey because of its much larger sample size. An
L427:        over-the-month employment change of about 122,000 is statistically significant in
L428:        the establishment survey, while the threshold for a statistically significant change
L429:        in the household survey is about 650,000. However, the household survey has a more
L430:        expansive scope than the establishment survey because it includes self-employed
L431:        workers whose businesses are unincorporated, unpaid family workers, agricultural
L432:        workers, and private household workers, who are excluded by the establishment survey.
L433:        The household survey also provides estimates of employment for demographic groups.
L434:        For more information on the differences between the two surveys, please visit
L435:        www.bls.gov/web/empsit/ces_cps_trends.htm.
L436:     2. Are undocumented immigrants counted in the surveys?
L437: 
L438:        It is likely that both surveys include at least some undocumented immigrants. However,
L439:        neither the establishment nor the household survey is designed to identify the legal
L440:        status of workers. Therefore, it is not possible to determine how many are counted in
L441:        either survey. The establishment survey does not collect data on the legal status of
L442:        workers. The household survey does include questions which identify the foreign and
L443:        native born, but it does not include questions about the legal status of the foreign
L444:        born. Data on the foreign and native born are published each month in table A-7 of
L445:        The Employment Situation news release.
L446: 
L447:     3. Why does the establishment survey have revisions?
L448: 
L449:        The establishment survey revises published estimates to improve its data series by
L450:        incorporating additional information that was not available at the time of the
L451:        initial publication of the estimates. The establishment survey revises its initial
L452:        monthly estimates twice, in the immediately succeeding 2 months, to incorporate
L453:        additional sample receipts from respondents in the survey and recalculated seasonal
L454:        adjustment factors. For more information on the monthly revisions, please visit
L455:        www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cestn.htm#Revisions-Between-Preliminary-and-Final-Data.
L456: 
L457:        On an annual basis, the establishment survey incorporates a benchmark revision that
L458:        re-anchors estimates to nearly complete employment counts available from unemployment
L459:        insurance tax records. The benchmark helps to control for sampling and modeling errors
L460:        in the estimates. For more information on the annual benchmark revision, please visit
L461:        www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesbmart.htm.
L462:     4. Does the establishment survey sample include small firms?
